newsitem.title: JAPAN: Clarke sees UK business in Japan pensions.
newsitem.headline: Clarke sees UK business in Japan pensions.

text.p: British financial institutions' biggest opportunities from Japanese deregulation will come in the areas of pension fund management, insurance, and large equity flotations, British finance minister Kenneth Clarke said on Friday.

"We have huge expertise in fund management for pension funds, particularly international management of pension funds, which I think the Japanese will have to resort to more and more as they remove the present restrictions," Clarke told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

"We have huge expertise in the insurance market, where again we can improve the performance of Japanese insurance funds if they use London to take advantage of our considerable ability as fund managers," Clarke said.

"If they are going for large equity flotations in things like Japanese railways and the Japanese telecommunications system, then London provides the best place in which to access international markets. And with the Japanese market being somewhat depressed at the moment I think they might be well advised to go to international markets and are bound to find London the best route to do so," he added.

Earlier on Friday Clarke told British reporters that he was "pretty confident" that Japan would make some large-scale equity issues in 1997 and use London to place a bigger proportion of those flotations in international markets.
Clarke arrived late on Wednesday for meetings with Japanese business executives and Japanese officials.

He said the main purposes of his visit were to get to know Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who took office late last year, to discuss the state of the Japanese economy and Japanese plans for deregulation and economic restructuring.
Clarke also told the British reporters he had asked why Japan could not immediately remove remaining restrictions on pension fund management and how quickly securities deregulation would take place.
"It is quite clear that Japan is not contemplating waiting for everything until 2001," he said.

"The impression I've formed so far is that the ministers are not contemplating just a bit by bit process toward 2001. I've been reassured that there is a genuine commitment to administrative reform and a desire to get on with it."
